scenes.title: A thread executes the GPU program.
The CPU supplies the launch and count.
A bounds check protects the arrays.
Three blocks cover all nine inputs.

cues.text: Chapter One starts with five floating-point inputs: one, two, three, four and five. Doubling gives two, four, six, eight and ten.
PyTorch chooses the implementation for its tensor operation. Our manual CUDA example performs the same calculation, so we can trace how each result is produced.
A thread is one execution of a GPU program. In this example, each participating thread reads one input, doubles it and writes the matching output position.
Thread four reads input index four, whose value is five. It writes ten at output index four. An index chooses a position; it is not the stored value.
With four threads per block, local positions start again at zero in each block. Block one, position zero therefore needs a global array index.
Multiply the block number by the block size, then add the local position. One times four plus zero gives index four, so this thread doubles the fifth input.
The CPU requests two blocks of four threads and passes an input count of five. The eight launched threads have indices zero through seven.
The count is an ordinary kernel argument supplied by the CPU program. Changing the number of blocks does not change that count or allocate longer arrays.
The correct check permits only indices smaller than five: zero through four. Threads five, six and seven skip both the read and the write.
A check allowing index five would access positions that do not exist. The guard trusts the supplied count; the CPU must also provide enough input and output storage.
Now there are nine inputs, with indices zero through eight. Keep four threads per block. Would two blocks cover every input?
Predict the smallest block count that covers all nine values. Which launched indices must then skip the arrays? Pause before comparing.
Two blocks create only eight threads, leaving input index eight without a thread. Three blocks create twelve threads, covering all nine inputs.
With the count set to nine, indices nine, ten and eleven skip the arrays. A bounds check can prevent an access, but it cannot create a missing thread.
Keep three questions separate: which input does this thread select, how many threads did the CPU launch, and which indices may safely access the arrays?
Return to Chapter One and compare four with eight threads per block. Explain why the grouping changes while each valid input still produces the same doubled result.
